definition: In Euclidean geometry, linear separability is a property of two sets of points.
details: This is most easily visualized in two dimensions (the Euclidean plane) by thinking of one set of points as being colored blue and the other set of points as being colored red. These two sets are linearly separable if there exists at least one line in the plane with all of the blue points on one side of the line and all the red points on the other side. This idea immediately generalizes to higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces if the line is replaced by a hyperplane. The problem of determining if a pair of sets is linearly separable and finding a separating hyperplane if they are, arises in several areas. In statistics and machine learning, classifying certain types of data is a problem for which good algorithms exist that are based on this concept.

explainer.lead: Linear separability is a property of two sets of points: whether a line, or a hyperplane in higher dimensions, can put all points of one set on one side and all of the other set on the other side. It matters because it determines when a linear decision boundary can separate the classes.

tiers.eli5: Imagine blue dots and red dots on paper; they are linearly separable if you can draw one straight line with all blue on one side and all red on the other.
tiers.practitioner: Determining whether a dataset is linearly separable informs whether a linear model can suffice; a pitfall is assuming separability in two dimensions carries over to higher dimensions without checking with a hyperplane.
tiers.paperLevel: Two sets in Euclidean space are linearly separable if a line (or hyperplane in higher dimensions) exists with each set entirely on one side.

explainer.example: In the plane, blue and red point sets are linearly separable if a single straight line puts all blue points on one side and all red points on the other.
